title: Zapatha v. Dairy Mart, Inc.
lead: Dairy Mart terminated a franchise after its operators declined a replacement agreement. On the disclosed terms and proven circumstances, Massachusetts’s highest court upheld the ninety-day termination power.

actors.name: Dairy Mart
actors.role: Owner of the premises and business equipment and franchisor

proceedings: Trial court enjoined termination and required good cause, with related chapter 93A relief.
Dairy Mart obtained direct appellate review.
Supreme Judicial Court reversed the judgments August 5, 1980.
limits: Record-specific rejection of unconscionability, bad faith, and unfair or deceptive conduct; no universal immunity for termination clauses. Article 2 principles applied by analogy, not direct coverage of the whole franchise.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The couple chooses a franchise
paragraphs: After losing his electroplating management job in May 1973, Bernard Zapatha sought a stable business of his own. He had a year of college, evening business-administration and business-law courses, and experience supervising up to 150 employees. Dairy Mart’s sales materials promised independence, security, and ownership. It approved an Agawam store and presented its form agreement November 8.

A representative read and explained the termination term, recommended legal advice, and said the terms were nonnegotiable. Bernard and Elaine signed without counsel. Bernard later testified that he understood every word but believed Dairy Mart could terminate only for cause. The actual term allowed either side, after the first twelve months, to terminate on ninety days’ written notice. Separate immediate-default provisions were not at issue.

Dairy Mart supplied equipped premises, paid rent, utilities, and some expenses, and licensed its name and methods in exchange for a percentage of gross sales. The couple bought inventory and paid wages and taxes. Upon no-cause termination, Dairy Mart would repurchase saleable inventory at retail less twenty percent. In 1974 the couple voluntarily moved to the Wilbraham Road store in Springfield and signed the same form.

sections.title: A proposed new contract leads to notice
sections.cue: The trial court protects continued operation
paragraphs: In November 1977 Dairy Mart proposed more detailed terms. Bernard objected to possible relocation, longer daily opening hours, and responsibility for future utility increases, choosing the existing agreement instead. Dairy Mart gave ninety days’ notice January 20, 1978, offered to purchase inventory, and invited discussions of a possible new agreement without promising terms or execution. No evidence showed the couple pursued compromise.

They sued to enjoin termination. The trial judge found rejection of the new agreement was the sole reason for notice and otherwise found no unconscionable or bad-faith conduct. Yet the judge held the termination clause unconscionable, imposed a good-cause requirement, and found violations of good faith and Massachusetts chapter 93A’s prohibition of unfair or deceptive conduct. Because the couple kept operating during suit, the separate statutory judgment apparently awarded only costs and attorney fees. Dairy Mart secured direct appellate review.

sections.title: Formation and performance require separate inquiries
paragraphs: Justice Wilkins’s Supreme Judicial Court opinion declined to treat the whole business-format franchise as a sale of goods under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2. About seventy percent of inventory came from others, and Dairy Mart principally received franchise fees. Splitting the agreement risked inconsistent rules. The court instead borrowed unconscionability and good-faith policies by common-law analogy.

Unconscionability concerned formation, commercial context, unfair surprise, and oppression. No one challenged ninety days as unreasonable notice. The term was plain, explained, and not hidden; the couple had time and declined recommended advice. Bernard’s education, experience, and subjective misunderstanding did not establish unfair surprise, even though negotiation was unavailable.

Nor did the record show an oppressive forfeiture. Dairy Mart owned the principal business assets and conceded it must buy all saleable inventory, including outside purchases, at eighty percent of retail. No unrecovered special equipment, insufficient recoupment period, or disproportionate risk unrelated to commercial needs was shown. The operators kept profits earned through the contractual term.

sections.title: Using the right was not proven unfair here
paragraphs: A fair term could still be used unfairly, so the court separately examined performance. No evidence identified or established violation of reasonable commercial standards. Dairy Mart openly invoked the agreed power after the couple refused new terms. Even an arguably arbitrary choice was not shown dishonest. Brochure claims of ownership were misleading, but the contracts disclosed Dairy Mart’s ownership and termination power, so those claims did not prove dishonesty concerning this termination.

Broader common-law fairness and chapter 93A yielded the same result. The court distinguished Fortune, the precedent protecting an employee from termination designed to withhold earned commissions: Dairy Mart appropriated no earned income or money reasonably due. No independently developed goodwill, special trade-building efforts, or unrecoverable investment was demonstrated. Massachusetts regulated some particular franchises but had not imposed cause on all of them; another state’s contrary franchise policy did not control. No cited federal regulatory interpretation made these circumstances deceptive.

The court reversed the judgments protecting the Zapathas. On this record Dairy Mart lawfully terminated; the decision neither ordered more factfinding nor declared every express termination clause immune from good-faith review.
